# Introduction 3

In analytics, the typical work flow starts with taking a data set and preparing it for further analysis. The objectives of analysis will typically determine the type of models that are to be fitted or the visualizations that will be created which all set forth the requirements for formatting the data. Given similar data sets and formatting requirements, the task of preparation may see an opportunity for automation. 


The wlsd (wrangling longitudinal survival data) package in R was designed with the intention to ease the process of formatting longitudinal data sets for models in the realm of survival analysis. Preparation may require intimate knowledge of the models and requirements of the data in order to fit so the functions in this package seek to ease with some of the work while also shedding more light onto some of these details.


This vignette will introduce some models used in survival analysis and the formats they require for fitting and then showcase some of the available features with this package through some examples.

# Introduction

Survival analysis is a branch of statistical modeling concerned with the study of time-to-event data (citation needed). However, there are very many techniques and methods for analyzing data in the context of survival whether it be with time or without time. (Author of multivariate survival analysis) uses a continuous time markov model in order to analyze time-to-event data where there exist more than 2 events. Removing time from analysis can lead to many traditional regression models being viewed as survival analysis tools. The odds or relative risk from logistic regression and Poisson regression respectively can be used for predicting survival and therefore could be categorized under this framework. This umbrella discipline of models became the bulk of discussion within my Master's thesis analyzing survival data from the perspective of different survival analysis models. 


As an ancillary project, the `wlsd` package was developed to support the processing of necessary data. The transformation and preparation tasks were performed many times on many data sets that it seemed right to introduce functional programming to improve on the repetition. After that thought it seemed right to just turn it into a package. 

Transitioning between different data formats requires detailed knowledge on how information is parsed and how variables are treated. The `wlsd` package in R provides methods for transforming data between different usable formats in an effort to ease this process. `wlsd` can transition between the counting process format and longitudinal or panel format. 



## Data Formats


A longitudinal study or panel study is a repeated observation method by which to investigate some phenomenon [@grillpanellong]. In other words, it analyzes subjects over time. These studies are often carried out over large periods of time with variables of interest being measured at snapshots of the process for each subject [@msmvignette]. In economics, panel data is used widely to analyze things such as labor markets [@frees2004]. Panel data also sees application to disease progression such as heart deterioration after transplant [@msmvignette]. For our purposes, the terms, longitudinal and panel, are interchangeable as they are effectively the same. A more technical definition is given by @frees2004 who defines both terms differently but also uses them interchangeably. We refer to the data generated by a longitudinal study or panel study as longitudinal data or panel data.


The three main requirements for longitudinal data are:

1. a subject identifier - this is some distinct index by which each entity under observation may be distinguished
2. time - the passage of events must be recorded in some manner
3. subject related variables - any other information pertaining to the subject and or time of observation


As most longitudinal studies involve many subjects, such as multiple patients in a medical study, longitudinal data will have a subject identifier. This may be a name or a number depending on the setup of the study but the manner in which subjects are identified is not usually relevant so long as different subjects can be differentiated from one another. Time is another requirement that may be recorded differently based on the data collection methods. It may be recorded using dates with or without cloak adjustments or as a duration.  All other variables should be tied to the subject but they may or may not be dependent on time. In the one case, there may be some variables that are constant throughout the study and do not change with time such as the type of medication taken during a drug trial. These are sometimes referred to as time independent variables or constant variables ??? I do not really have a citation???. The other case sees variables that do change with the subject over time. This may include something such as age. These are sometimes referred to time dependent variables or non-constant variables ???. While not all variables are required to fall in one case or another and most studies will have a mix of types, they will all usually have at least one variable that is time dependent as this motivates the need for repeated observations over time.


There exist at least several different data formats for organizing longitudinal data. Those used by `wlsd` will be covered in the remainder of this section. This list is not exhaustive and represents a subset of applicable formats as survival analysis is a large discipline and may contain many more data formats. Previous work for @mythesis motivated the current list and future work may seek to expand it but suggestions for additions are appreciated.


### Long Format


The first format to be discussed is arguably one of the most common which is known as the long format. This format is organized such that each row represents a different observation over time. It is a very natural format for data keeping as at a particular time point the relevant observational information can be recorded in the row. All other information can be stored in additional columns relating to that subject and time.


A small toy example is produced below. Consider 3 individuals whose subject identifier is denoted by `id` and observation time by `time`. In this example, time is represented as some number of units from the start of the study. Each individual starts at time 0 and subsequent values of time are interpreted as the number of units since time 0. Here, units can mean something like the number of days or minutes since the start. Additionally, there are 3 other variables, `event`, `var1`, and `var2`, respectively. The variables `event` and `var1` vary with time for each individual and `var2` is constant over time for the subjects.



```{r long-tab, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
knitr::kable(long_data, caption = "Long Format Data", label = "long-tab")
```


Inspection of the long format table above shows the row-wise passage of time for each subject with corresponding observation values within each column. This format is easily legible and can be readily filtered. Using the first row as an example, the interpretation of the data shows that subject 1 had an observation at time 0 according to `time` with relevant values of 0 and 10.4 for `event` and `var1`, respectively. Additionally, the constant variable, `var2`, is 10 which applies to all rows for the subject.

### Wide Format

The complement to the long format is called wide format where the time variables are expressed as multiple columns of observations instead of multiple rows. Each subject contributes only 1 row of data. All time independent variables have a single column whose value is representative for all time points. The time dependent variables have multiple columns whose value represents the observation at a particular time. The number of columns for each time dependent variable is equal to the maximum number of observations for any one subject. 


The wide format table below displays the same data as shown in long format table but now translated for wide format. 

```{r wide-tab, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
knitr::kable(wide_data, caption = "Wide Format Data")
```


The relevant observational information is now shown across multiple columns for the multiple time points. Initially, there were 3 time dependent variables. The long format table showed each variable had their own column in the long format. Now, in the wide format, the time dependent variables have multiple columns for each observation. There are 3 time dependent variables that now contribute 4 columns each for a total of 12 time dependent columns in the wide format table. This is because individual 1 had 4 time observations that are now translated from rows to columns. A number was appended to the original column name in order to indicate to which observation the column values correspond. Since the number of columns is determined by the maximum observations for a subject, some columns might have missing information as the subject did not have an observation. Subjects that did not have observations at these times have the values as missing denoted by `NA` in order to maintain consistency across the shape of the table. 


Interpretation for observations becomes a bit more cumbersome as you have to look at the correct column to discern time dependent values. All of the relevant information for a subject is located within that subject row. For the first observation of subject 1, you have to look at the relevant row for the first column of each variable. This would be `time1`, `event1` and `var11`. The constant variable `var2` has the same value for each time point so only has 1 column.


This format is not currently supported by the `wlsd` package but may see inclusion in the future. See @mstatevignette for an example of wide format data in application of multi-state models.





### Counting Process Format

The most frequently used data format for survival analysis is the counting process format. This is a longitudinal data format characterized by a series of time intervals. Each row corresponds to a different time interval where the start and stop points are defined by columns. All other columns represent different variable values associated with the interval and or subject. Observations typically occur at the end of the interval therefore, any time dependent variables are taken to be the value recorded at the stop point of the time interval. Constant variables are time invariant and remain the same for the subject over all time intervals ergo all subject rows. The table below shows an example of counting process format using the data from our previous examples.



```{r cp-tab, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
knitr::kable(cp_data, caption = "Counting Process Format")
```


Here, the time information has been split into two columns, namely `time1` and `time2`, defining our interval. Mathematically, the interval is right-open. That is, $(time1, time2] = \{x|time1 < x \leq time2\}$. So, multiple time intervals for a particular subject will not overlap. As noted previously, other variables for a subject are taken to be observed at the end of the interval. An example interpretation for the first row is subject 1 started their first interval after time 0 and ended it at time 31 at which point their `event` is 0 and `var1` is 11.3. The constant, `var2`, is 10 regardless of time. Note that this data format has 1 less observation for each subject than previous formats. Since observed values are taken at the end of the interval, the format does not contain information about observed values of the starting time point of the first interval. This consideration becomes important when performing data transitions. 


A detailed description of the counting process format is given by @collett in its use for survival analysis. @survival-vignette also gives a description of the counting process format with use case examples on how it is leveraged in survival analysis.




### Count Format

Count data looks at frequencies of quantifiable values within some interval. While not a traditional survival analysis format, count data may provide useful insights into a subject's survival through relationships among aggregated counts of events. Relevant data may include counted occurrences of a disease with associated covariates. Any meaningful insights in counts might, at the very least, point further survival analysis into a  particular direction. Based on these remarks, it is argued that the count data is a type of longitudinal data that can be used for survival analysis and is included in this package. 



The count format is straightforward as each row will be for a particular subject and all other variables will either be constant or aggregations of their time points. The table below shows the example data set in count format. 


```{r count-tab, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
knitr::kable(count_data, caption = "Count Format Data")
```


Each subject has their own row where the `event` column now counts each subjects number of events. Since each subject had only one event, the result is a column of ones. The constant variables are simplified to one row for each subject as they do not vary over time. The time dependent variables, that do not include `event`, require adjustment as there is only one row for each subject under this format. For each of the other dependent variables, a statistic is chosen to represent the variable. In the case of `time`, the maximum value for each subject is taken. This gives the last time point recorded for observation and can be used as a reference for the time interval with which counts were taken. The `var1` summary uses the mean to take an average value for each subject. Thus, individual 1 had only 1 event after 96 time units with an average `var1` of `r round(mean(c(10.4, 11.3, 12.7, 17.5)),2)` and a constant `var2` of 10. 

## Data Transitions

The discussion of data formats gives motivation for the data transitions that are available in the package. Figure ??? shows the available transitions within the package for the data formats discussed thus far.


```{r transition_graphic, echo=FALSE, out.width="50%", fig.cap="Format transitions for wlsd."}
knitr::include_graphics("../man/figures/wlsd-format-drawing.png")
```



In the figure above, transitions possible through `wlsd` are denoted by an arrow. The wide format does not currently have functions for transition so it remains isolated from the rest of the formats. The solid arrows represent explicitly defined transitions while the single dashed arrow represents a transition that is possible but does not have its own function for use. This is transition is discussed a bit more in the "long2count()" section below.

### Long Format to Counting Process Format


The first transition to be discussed is the long format to counting process format transition. The `long2cp()` function is used for this operation and works through the code below.

```{r long2cp}
long2cp(data = long_data, id = "id", time = "time")
```
It requires `data`, `id`, and `time` arguments by default. Using the data from the long format example earlier, the function will transition data to the counting process format.


By default, the function will keep all subjects through the `drop = FALSE` argument. However, it may be desirable to drop individuals that only have 1 row of data in long format as they do not have enough information for time intervals. Consider the `dropped_long` data set below which is missing the 2nd observation for `id` 3. This subject has only one time point so a start and stop time interval is not really feasible. However, to maintain the data set that is input to `long2cp()`, the subject is kept in the output data set with a time interval that starts and stops at the one time point given. All covariates are then associated with that one point.

```{r long2cp no drop}
dropped_long <- long_data[1:8,]
long2cp(dropped_long, id = "id", time = "time", drop = "FALSE")
```

If the subject is intended to be dropped for analysis purposes, then the `drop = TRUE` argument can be used to exclude these rows from the output data set.

```{r long2cp drop}
long2cp(dropped_long, id = "id", time = "time", drop = "TRUE")
```

The single row for `id` 3 is missing in the output above. 

### Counting Process Format to Long Format

The transition from counting process format to long format is done through the `cp2long()` function. Arguments are similar to the previous function but take two time points as input instead of one. This is to consolidate the two end points of the interval into a single column.

```{r cp2long}
cp2long(data = cp_data, id = "id", time1 = "time1", time2 = "time2")
```

Note that in this example there are a few `NA` values which differ from the example counting process table. This is due to the missing information about the first time covariates mentioned earlier. By default, the function will not make any assumptions about this data and will simply leave `NA` values. If desired, the `fill = TRUE` option may be used in order to insert values for any constant columns.


```{r cp2long fill}
cp2long(cp_data, id = "id", time1 = "time1", time2 = "time2", fill = TRUE)
```

Here, the `var2` column was constant and `NA` values were populated.

### Long Format to Count Format

The transitions to count format are done through the `long2count()` function. While originally conceived to perform the transition from long format to count format, the logic here is the same as that in the counting process format to count format so this function can be used for both transitions. The major difference between the long format and counting process format is how time is organized so the logic of aggregating any covariates row-wise should be the same.


The `long2count()` function requires a data set and identifier to perform aggregation operations. It also requires an argument to either the `event` or `state` argument. This will determine how to treat events of interest under the observation scheme of the data set. The `event` argument will treat the given column or columns as numeric counts of observations while the `state` argument will treat the column largely as a factor with different levels. 


Consider the first example below with the long format data and the single event column called "event".

```{r long2count}
long2count(long_data, id = "id", event = "event")
```
Since argument supplied to `event` was a count of occurrences, the output column is a sum of rows. Any columns that are constant within the `id` argument grouping are carried over to the output as is while any that are time varying (or change row-wise) are then aggregated into the final count format output.


The default aggregation function for any time varying covariate is `mean()` but this can be changed through the `FUN` argument. For example, setting `FUN = max` will take the maximum value over time and use that as value in the aggregated count data set.


```{r long2count fun}
long2count(long_data, id = "id", event = "event", FUN = max)
```


For multiple events, the concatenated names of event columns can be supplied to the `event` argument.

```{r long2count events}
long_data2 <- long_data
long_data2$event2 <- c(2,2,3,1,2,3,2,1,3)
long2count(long_data2, id = "id", event = c("event","event2"))
```


If the observational thing is to be treated as a state instead of an event, then the state argument will handle the aggregations as such. Consider the `event` column as a binary state such that "0" is coded as healthy and "1" is coded for unhealthy. The state argument will instead count the number of occurrences of each state.

```{r long2count state}
long2count(long_data, id = "id", state = "event")
```

For the example above, subject 1 now has two rows for each of the different levels of "event". From the "event.counts" column, this subject has 3 occurrences of state 0 being healthy and 1 occurrence of state 1 being unhealthy. This can be expanded to larger state spaces with more detailed descriptions.


An argument is required to be supplied to either the `event` or `state` argument. The `event` argument will handle multiple columns as events but the `state` argument will only accept one column to be treated as a state. Combinations of `event` and `state` are allowed such as 1 state and 1 event or 1 state and multiple events.


## Helper Functions


There exist a few other functions within the `wlsd` package to help with small niche cases that may arise in practice. They are all formalized functions based on preparations of the `LBP` data set (discussed later). The three notable functions are `basedate()`, `events2state()`, and `takefirst()`. The first, `basedate()`, creates a new row for each individual which can serve as their baseline or first visit and then be populated with new information. The `events2state()` function is meant to consolidate multiple columns of event observations to a single state column. That is, it aggregates multiple columns into a single factor-like column based on the combinations of values from the input columns. The `takefirst()` function takes the first number of rows for each subject up to and including a given criteria. These functions are discussed in greater detail in the "Applications" section below as the example context gives greater understanding to their use. 


# Applications
## Example: Low-Back Pain Analysis


In order to demonstrate the use cases of this package, consider this example using a low-back pain (LBP) data set to be prepared for several models in a larger survival analysis effort. The data set originally comes from @garg which was used in @mythesis for a comprehensive survival analysis where some of this example originates. See the appendix section for more discussion on data preparation using some early versions of this package.


The data is available within the package via `LBP`. It consists of 466 individuals with associated low back pain statuses over a 6 year observation period. The first 5 rows and the first 10 columns of data are shown below.

```{r LBP head}
LBP[1:5,1:10]
```

The data set is organized in long format with subject column `sid`, primary time column `time_to_row`, and several time varying LBP variables including `case.lbp`, `case.med`, `case.sc`, and `case.lt`. These last 4 variables represent the binary occurrence of LBP, LBP requiring medication, LBP requiring medical care, and LBP resulting in lost time from work, respectively, at the time of observation. See the help file via `help(LBP)` for more information. 


At the time of construction for this particular data set, the baseline data was not available. That is, the first observations were missing. For analysis purposes, the assumption was made that all individuals would be free from all LBP at this time point and the analysis would continue. That assumed information can be added to the data set through the `basedate()` function. In the code below, a new row is added for each individual that can then be populated with the new LBP values.


```{r baseline}
LBPwBaseline <- basedate(LBP, "sid")
LBPwBaseline[1:5,1:10]
```


As baseline information is unavailable, there are a few data points that require information. The baseline date for all individuals is stored as a constant in another column, `Baseline.date`. This data point can be dragged over to the baseline `Date` column for each individual. Subsequently, we can fill in 0s for all other missing data points as we will assume that each individual starts the study without any instances of the case definitions which is indicated by 0 and the baseline visit which is the first observation is time `time_to_row` equal to 0. 

```{r update baseline}
LBPwBaseline$Date <- ifelse(is.na(LBPwBaseline$Date), LBPwBaseline$Baseline.date, LBPwBaseline$Date)
LBPwBaseline[is.na(LBPwBaseline)] <- 0
```

Any constant columns within subject groups are carried over to the new row while anything that changes over time or row-wise, is left as `NA`. 


Through exploration, a few cases can be found where the "case.lbp" columns is 0 while another "case." column is 1. 

```{r 0 example}
LBPwBaseline[404:406,1:8]
```


Intuitively, this does not make sense as these other cases are defined to be based on the subject having LBP and therefore "case.lbp". This was most likely due to data entry errors for the "case.lbp" column so these are revalued to 1 if another case value is also 1.



```{r case progression}
LBPwBaseline$case.lbp <- ifelse(LBPwBaseline$case.lbp == 0 &
                               (LBPwBaseline$case.med == 1 | 
                                LBPwBaseline$case.sc == 1 | 
                                LBPwBaseline$case.lt == 1),
                                1, 
                                LBPwBaseline$case.lbp)
LBPwBaseline[404:406,1:8]
```



As is, the data set is in a format that can be used for a multi-state model analysis such as that provided by the `msm` package. The package uses a state argument which is taken as a single column. The multiple LBP columns cannot be passed in their current form. The `events2state()` function can be used to consolidate those multiple columns into a single column based on the different combinations of values.

```{r events2state}
LBP_msm <- events2state(LBPwBaseline, events = c("case.lbp",
                                                 "case.med",
                                                 "case.sc",
                                                 "case.lt"))
```

In the code above, the 4 given input columns have values which when combined give 9 total combinations. The combination levels are output to the console when the function runs. By default, these combinations are changed to numbers through the `number = TRUE` argument. The `interaction()` function handles the combinations of columns which by default drops unused combinations. That can be toggled in the `drop` argument.


The `LBP_msm` data set is suitable input for the `msm` package. This is largely the form used for the analysis in @mythesis which has a section on using the `msm` package for multi-state model analysis of this data set.



In order to transition the data set to counting process format, the `long2cp()` function is used below.

```{r LBP cp}
LBP_cp <- long2cp(LBPwBaseline, id = "sid", time = "time_to_row")
LBP_cp[1:5,1:10]
```

Any subjects with 1 row are dropped since they do not have enough time information for the desired analysis. The `survival` package contains analysis models that take data in counting process format as input. The `LBP_cp` data set has multiple occurrences of LBP so a repeated event or recurrent model might be more suitable.

If a simple Cox proportional-hazards model is desired, all observations after the first occurrence of LBP can be truncated using the `takefirst()` function. 


```{r takefirst}
LBP_cp2 <- takefirst(LBP_cp, id = "sid",
                     criteria.column = "case.lbp",
                     criteria = 1)

LBP_cp2[11:14,1:8]
```

In this form, `LBP_cp2` has all rows up to and including the first time "case.lbp" is 1 for each subject. From this point, the standard `coxph` functionality follows. 



The transitions to count format are done through `long2count()`. Only the LBP related values and time itself vary row-wise. As events, the LBP columns can be counted through the `event` argument as demonstrated below.


```{r LBP count}
LBP_count <- long2count(LBPwBaseline, "sid", event = c("case.lbp",
                                                 "case.med",
                                                 "case.sc",
                                                 "case.lt"))

LBP_count[1:5,c(1,20:24)]
```


If looking at the `LBP_msm` data set with the state column, the `state` argument can be used and we can sum all the LBP variables to count their occurrences over time.

```{r LBP state}
LBP_state <- long2count(LBP_msm, "sid", state = "state", FUN = sum)
LBP_state[1:9,c(1,5:8,24:26)]
```

In the case of using the `state` argument, all 9 states are counted for each subject. The other LBP columns are summed getting the total number of occurrences for each column. Either count format data set should be suitable for some sort of count regression model. The former might offer a more straightforward approach relating a single count to covariates of interest. The latter data set might be suitable with a random effect and a reduced state space.
See @mythesis for an example analysis using count regression on only the counts of "case.lbp".
